issues.legal_issue: Promoters may acquire property for a company before incorporation, with the benefit passing to the company after incorporation and acceptance of the transaction.
material_facts: The promoters acquired the property before the company was incorporated, describing themselves as its promoters or directors.

After incorporation, the company treated the property as its asset in corporate records, asserted ownership in litigation, used it as security for a loan, and paid the promoters the acquisition amount.
The company accepted the pre-incorporation transaction and communicated that acceptance by asserting ownership of the property.
issues.conclusion: The property was acquired for the benefit of the company, and its pre-incorporation status did not prevent the benefit of the acquisition from passing to it.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 15(h) and 19(e) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permit enforcement of a pre-incorporation contract made for a company’s purpose when the company accepts it and communicates acceptance. Section 5 of the Transfer of Property Act does not bar a transfer in favour of an unincorporated company. The Court relied on Weavers Mills Ltd. v. Balkis Ammal and Vali Pattabhirama Rao v. Sri Ramanuja Ginning & Rice Factory (P.) Ltd.; it also explained that Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act does not itself bar a benami transaction or determine whether the apparent state of affairs is the real one.

rule.if: pre_incorporation_company_benefit and company_later_incorporated and company_accepted_transaction and company_communicated_acceptance

predicates.pre_incorporation_company_benefit: Promoters acquired property before incorporation for the purposes or benefit of the proposed company.
predicates.company_later_incorporated: The proposed company was subsequently incorporated.
predicates.company_accepted_transaction: After incorporation, the company adopted or acted upon the property acquisition as its own transaction.
predicates.company_communicated_acceptance: The company communicated its acceptance of the transaction to the relevant other party, including by asserting its ownership.

issues.definition: When promoters acquire property for a proposed company and the company later accepts the transaction and communicates that acceptance, the benefit of the acquisition passes to the company.

issues.legal_issue: A person who represents that a company owns property and induces another to act on that representation may be estopped from later denying the company’s ownership.
material_facts: The promoters represented in court proceedings, corporate records, and dealings concerning a bank mortgage that the company owned the property.
The promoters signed the company’s pleadings and documents making or repeating those representations.
The purchasers relied on the representations when entering the sale transaction and paying an advance.
The Court found no statutory bar to vesting title in the company.
issues.conclusion: The promoters were estopped from denying or disputing the company’s title to the property.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principles of estoppel, acquiescence, and approbation and reprobation, including the rule reflected in Section 116 of the Evidence Act in appropriate circumstances. A mere admission does not create title, but conduct and representations are relevant to determining intention and may prevent a party from taking an inconsistent position where another has acted to their detriment. The Court relied on Bank of India v. O.P. Swarnakar, Gillett v. Holt, Indu Shekhar Singh v. State of U.P., Pawan Alloys v. U.P. State Electricity Board, Taylor Fashions Ltd. v. Liverpool Victoria Trustees Co. Ltd., Amalgamated Investment & Property Co. Ltd. v. Texas Commerce International Bank Ltd., and Sarat Chunder Dey v. Gopal Chunder Laha.

rule.if: property_ownership_dispute and party_represented_company_ownership and other_party_relied_on_representation_to_its_detriment and no_statutory_bar

predicates.property_ownership_dispute: The parties disputed who owned the property.
predicates.party_represented_company_ownership: A party represented that the company, rather than that party personally, owned the property.
predicates.other_party_relied_on_representation_to_: Another party relied on the representation and changed its position to its detriment.
predicates.no_statutory_bar: No statutory restriction prevented the company from holding title to the property.

issues.definition: If a party represents company ownership in a property dispute and another relies on that representation to their detriment, the party may be prevented from denying it when no statutory bar applies.

issues.legal_issue: A court may lift the corporate veil when those controlling a company use its separate personality to advance their own dishonest or fraudulent purposes.
material_facts: The promoters were the company’s only subscribers and shareholders, and they controlled its board with their son.
The promoters executed the disputed sale agreement as directors after the company had resolved to sell the property.
The Court found that the promoters used the company’s personality to further their personal objectives and fraudulent design.
issues.conclusion: The corporate veil was applicable to be lifted, and the promoters could not take a position inconsistent with the company’s interests by relying on its separate personality.
issues.legal_principle: The corporate veil may be pierced where a corporate entity is abused for an unjust or inequitable purpose, so that the court can identify those responsible. The Court relied on Kapila Hingorani v. State of Bihar, State of U.P. v. Renusagar Power Co., Union of India v. Playworld Electronics Pvt. Ltd., and Yukong Line Ltd. v. Rendsburg Investments Corp.

predicates.company_control_dispute: The dispute concerns conduct undertaken through a company and the relationship between the company and its controllers.
predicates.company_controlled_by_claiming_parties: The parties whose conduct is challenged controlled the company and its decision-making.
predicates.corporate_personality_used_for_personal_: The controllers used the company’s separate personality to advance their own dishonest or fraudulent purpose.

issues.definition: Where parties controlling a company use its corporate personality for their own fraudulent purpose, the court may look beyond that personality to assess their conduct.

issues.legal_issue: A party may challenge a decree as fraudulent in a collateral proceeding despite withdrawing an earlier suit that sought to set the decree aside.
material_facts: The purchasers had filed a suit challenging an arbitral award and a decree as fraudulent, then withdrew that suit.
They had already obtained a decree for specific performance in the suit in which they raised the fraud challenge.
The trial court found that material facts had been concealed and that the decree resulted from a collusive and fraudulent proceeding.
issues.conclusion: Withdrawal of the earlier suit did not prevent the purchasers from raising the fraud challenge in the specific-performance proceeding; a decree obtained by fraud could be treated as a nullity there.
issues.legal_principle: Section 44 of the Evidence Act permits a party to show that a judgment or decree was obtained by fraud or collusion in a proceeding in which it is relied upon. Fraud vitiates solemn acts, and a plea of fraud may be raised collaterally. The Court rejected the contention that Order 23, Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure barred the challenge after withdrawal, and relied on Ram Chandra Singh v. Savitri Devi, Vice Chairman, Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan v. Girdhari Lal Yadav, State of A.P. v. T. Suryachandra Rao, Ishwar Dutt v. Land Acquisition Collector, and the other fraud authorities cited in the judgment.

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding in which the challenge is raised seeks specific performance of a contract.
predicates.prior_suit_to_set_aside_decree_withdrawn: The party previously filed, and later withdrew, a suit seeking to set aside the decree.
predicates.decree_relied_on_alleged_to_be_fraudulen: The party alleges that the decree relied on in the current proceeding was obtained by fraud or collusion.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance proceeding, withdrawing an earlier suit to set aside a decree does not bar a collateral challenge alleging that the decree was obtained by fraud.

issues.legal_issue: A sale agreement is not converted into a loan agreement merely because it provides for repayment of an advance with interest if title defects or legal obstacles arise.
material_facts: The written agreement described a sale of the property for an agreed price and provided for payment of the balance on execution and registration of the sale deed.
A clause allowed the purchasers to seek return of the advance with interest if a defect in title, encumbrance, or legal obstacle was found.
The property had been mortgaged, and part of the advance was used to discharge the company’s bank debt.
The Court found no other legal evidence establishing that the transaction was a loan.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was an agreement for sale, not a loan transaction.
issues.legal_principle: A title-protection clause providing for return of an advance with interest does not, without more, turn a sale agreement into a loan. Inadequate consideration alone is not proof of a loan and is not by itself a ground to refuse specific performance; Section 20, Explanation 1 of the Specific Relief Act also states that mere inadequacy of consideration does not constitute an unfair advantage or hardship of the specified kind. The Court relied on P.D’Souza v. Shondrilo Naidu and distinguished the suggestion drawn from the disputed alternative agreement.

predicates.agreement_for_sale_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a written property transaction is a sale agreement or a loan.
predicates.written_agreement_sets_sale_price_and_sa: The writing states a sale price and obligations directed toward completing a sale.
predicates.refund_clause_only_protects_against_titl: The refund provision applies to defects in title, encumbrances, or legal obstacles to the sale.
predicates.no_other_legal_evidence_of_loan: No other legal evidence establishes that the parties intended a loan.

issues.definition: A writing structured as a sale remains a sale agreement where its refund clause protects against title or legal defects and there is no other legal evidence of a loan.

issues.legal_issue: An agreement to sell a house includes the land appurtenant to it unless the agreement expressly excludes the land.
material_facts: The agreement referred to the house or bungalow on the property.
The sellers had acquired the house property together with the land, and the agreement contained no express exclusion of the land.
The dispute concerned whether the agreement covered only the structure or also the land.
issues.conclusion: The agreement covered both the house and the land.
issues.legal_principle: The word “house” may include appurtenant land, and a building ordinarily includes the land on which it stands unless the parties expressly stipulate otherwise. The Court relied on the definitions cited from legal lexicons and T. Lakshmipathi v. P. Nithyananda Reddy.

predicates.agreement_scope_dispute: The parties dispute what property is covered by an agreement concerning a house.
predicates.agreement_refers_to_house_on_land: The agreement refers to a house or building situated on land acquired or held with it.
predicates.no_express_exclusion_of_land: The agreement contains no express term excluding the land from the transaction.

issues.definition: When an agreement concerning a house does not expressly exclude its land, the agreement covers the house and its appurtenant land.

issues.legal_issue: The party seeking specific performance may be found responsible for demolition on the balance of the circumstances even when criminal proceedings concerning the demolition remain pending.
material_facts: The building was demolished on the day possession was delivered under an ex parte order obtained in a rent proceeding.
The purchasers were not armed with that possession order, while the opposing parties were.
A charge-sheet accused the purchasers of demolition and related offences, but criminal proceedings were still pending.
The circumstances, including the purchasers’ connection with the person who brought the rent proceeding, led the Court to uphold the finding against them for disposal of the civil case.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the finding, for purposes of the case, that the purchasers were responsible for demolishing the building, while not expressing a final opinion on the pending criminal case.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the sequence of events and the balance of the available circumstances in the civil dispute, without treating the pending charge-sheet as conclusive proof. It relied on the circumstances surrounding possession, demolition, and the parties’ conduct, and expressly left the criminal case undecided.

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The proceeding seeks specific performance of a property-sale agreement.
predicates.building_demolished_during_possession_di: A building was demolished amid competing claims to possession of the property.
predicates.demolition_circumstances_tilt_against_cl: The sequence of events and other circumstances weigh against the party seeking specific performance as responsible for the demolition.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance proceeding, the claimant may be found responsible for demolition for purposes of the civil dispute when the surrounding circumstances weigh against that claimant.

issues.legal_issue: A court may refuse specific performance and award monetary compensation instead when the parties’ serious misconduct and the circumstances make specific enforcement inequitable.
material_facts: Both sides initiated numerous proceedings, suppressed material facts, and abused the judicial process.
The Court found the purchasers responsible for demolishing the building for purposes of the case.
The purchasers had paid a substantial advance, and the property’s value had risen substantially.
The Court found both sides blameworthy and concluded that monetary relief would better balance the equities than compelling a sale.
issues.conclusion: The Court refused specific performance and directed repayment of the advance with interest and payment of additional compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 makes specific performance discretionary and requires the discretion to be sound and guided by judicial principles; it permits refusal in specified circumstances of unfair advantage, hardship, or inequity. Compensation may be awarded in substitution for specific performance, with the amount and form of relief assessed in light of the circumstances and balance of hardship. The Court relied on Snell’s Equity, Spry’s Equitable Remedies, Gillett v. Holt, Malhotra v. Choudhury, Lalit Kumar Jain v. Jaipur Traders Corporation, P.D’Souza v. Shondrilo Naidu, Nirmala Anand v. Advent Corporation, and Surinder Singh v. Kapoor Singh.

rule.if: specific_performance_proceeding and serious_misconduct_by_both_sides and claimant_responsible_for_demolition_for_civil_dispute and monetary_relief_can_balance_the_equities

predicates.specific_performance_proceeding: The claimant seeks specific performance of a property-sale agreement.
predicates.serious_misconduct_by_both_sides: Both sides engaged in serious misconduct, including abuse of the judicial process or suppression of material facts.
predicates.claimant_responsible_for_demolition_for_: The claimant was found responsible for demolition of the building for purposes of the civil dispute.
predicates.monetary_relief_can_balance_the_equities: The circumstances permit monetary relief to address the parties’ competing interests more fairly than specific enforcement.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks specific performance, both sides have engaged in serious misconduct, the claimant is responsible for demolition, and monetary relief can balance the equities, the court may deny specific performance and award compensation instead.
